THOUGHT: The clinical picture—sharply demarcated erythematous scaly plaques with fissuring confined to a digit, prominent nail changes (pitting), long history of “eczema” from childhood, poor response to topical corticosteroids, and development of a new psoriatic plaque elsewhere after treatment—strongly suggests a psoriatic disorder rather than contact/irritant dermatitis. The described histopathology (neutrophil‑rich spongiform pustules within the epidermis, dermal edema, lymphohistiocytic infiltrate; nail bed with acanthosis and spongiform pustules) is classic for pustular psoriasis (spongiform pustules of Kogoj). The localization to a finger with confluent involvement and nail involvement fits acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau (a localized pustular psoriasis of the digits). Patch testing was negative, lowering likelihood of allergic contact dermatitis. Alternative considerations include other forms of pustular or chronic plaque psoriasis, chronic hand eczema (atopic/irritant), and tinea manuum, but histology and nail findings point firmly toward a pustular psoriatic etiology.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau (localized pustular psoriasis of the digits)
2. Palmoplantar pustulosis (pustular psoriasis localized to palms/soles)
3. Chronic plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris of the hand)
4. Chronic hand eczema (atopic or irritant dermatitis)
5. Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection of the hand)
